extracted.intended_audience: students of political economy; policymakers; informed general readers interested in public finance
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of taxation and public revenue
extracted.subtask_description: A normative and descriptive account of different forms of taxation (capitation, taxes on consumables, excise, customs), their incidence, administrative modes, and their economic and social effects. The text explains how taxes fall on different social classes, how they affect wages, consumption, smuggling, and public revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitation taxes characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitation taxes are levied at little expense; and, where they are rigorously exacted, afford a very sure revenue to the state. It is upon this account that, in countries where the case, comfort, and security of the inferior ranks of people are little attended to, capitation taxes are very common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes both administrative ease and political/regressive consequences: capitation is cheap to collect and reliable for revenue but places direct burdens on lower ranks and is only a small part of public revenue in large states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on consumable commodities as indirect taxation of revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The state not knowing how to tax, directly and proportionably, the revenue of its subjects, endeavours to tax it indirectly by taxing their expense, which, it is supposed, will, in most cases, be nearly in proportion to their revenue. Their expense is taxed, by taxing the consumable commodities upon which it is laid out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames excises/customs as a proxy for income taxation; implies criterion that indirect taxes should be assessed with awareness of their imperfect proportionality to actual revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of necessaries vs luxuries (by custom and decency)
rubrics_metrics.description: By necessaries I understand, not only the commodities which are indispensibly necessary for the support of life, but whatever the custom of the country renders it indecent for creditable people, even of the lowest order, to be without... All other things I call luxuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of 'necessary' is context-dependent (custom, decency); examples: linen shirts and leather shoes are necessaries in Britain but not universally. Policy implication: taxes on 'necessaries' affect different classes depending on local custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax on necessaries raises wages through higher subsistence costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax upon those articles necessarily raises their price somewhat higher than the amount of the tax, because the dealer, who advances the tax, must generally get it back, with a profit. Such a tax must, therefore, occasion a rise in the wages of labour, proportionable to this rise of price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: increased cost of subsistence → employers raise wages to compensate → wage rise is passed on via prices/profits/rent. Implication: taxing necessaries has economy-wide price-wage effects and overcharges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on luxuries need not raise wages
rubrics_metrics.description: It is otherwise with taxes upon what I call luxuries, even upon those of the poor. The rise in the price of the taxed commodities, will not necessarily occasion any rise in the wages of labour... those high duties seem to have no effect upon the wages of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tobacco, tea, sugar, chocolate taxed heavily yet wages unchanged. Policy implication: taxing luxuries is less likely to alter wage-setting and broader production prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on luxuries act as sumptuary laws and can alter consumption patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The high price of such commodities does not necessarily diminish the ability of the inferior ranks of people to bring up families. Upon the sober and industrious poor, taxes upon such commodities act as sumptuary laws, and dispose them either to moderate, or to refrain altogether from the use of superfluities which they can no longer easily afford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes effects on 'sober and industrious' poor (reducing wasteful consumption, possible net benefit) vs dissolute poor (may continue consumption at cost of family welfare). Use when assessing distributive/social effects of luxury taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes upon necessaries reduce ability to raise families unless wages rise proportionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rise in the average price of necessaries, unless it be compensated by a proportionable rise in the wages of labour, must necessarily diminish, more or less, the ability of the poor to bring up numerous families...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: ensure wage compensation if taxing necessities, or else anticipate demographic/labour-supply consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on necessaries raise prices of manufactures and reduce sales (overcharge and cascading taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes upon necessaries, by raising the wages of labour, necessarily tend to raise the price of all manufactures, and consequently to diminish the extent of their sale and consumption... certain taxes are, in the price of certain goods, sometimes repeated and accumulated four or five times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights incidence across production chain (tax stacking) and the disproportionate burden on landlords and consumers; use to evaluate whether tax design creates cascading overcharges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and roles of excise versus customs duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties of excise are imposed chiefly upon goods of home produce, destined for home consumption... The duties of customs are much more ancient... originally considered as taxes upon the profits of merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative and substantive distinction: excise is clearer in scope and levied on few widely used home goods; customs historically broader and often less precise. Relevant for choosing which instrument to use for revenue and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate mode of taxing by durability and consumption speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The consumable goods which last a considerable time before they are consumed altogether, are most properly taxed [by an annual sum]; those of which the consumption is either immediate or more speedy, [are taxed at dealer]. The coach-tax and plate tax are examples of the former method; the greater part of the other duties of excise and customs, of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: durable goods → annual/licence-style taxation; quickly consumed goods → tax at point-of-sale (excise/customs) to preserve convenience, piece-meal payment, and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems with licensing (annual payment) for quick-consumption goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The project... of taxing, in this manner, goods of immediate or speedy consumption, seems liable to the four following very important objections. First... inequality; Secondly... loss of piece-meal payment convenience; Thirdly... less sumptuary effect; Fourthly... lump payments might distress the workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four explicit objections to lump/licence taxes for consumables: (1) unequal burden relative to consumption, (2) removes voluntary piece-meal payment option, (3) undermines temperance incentives, (4) may cause hardship due to lump sums. Use to evaluate licensing proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: High duties may reduce revenue by diminishing consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: High taxes, sometimes by diminishing the consumption of the taxed commodities... frequently afford a smaller revenue to government than what might be drawn from more moderate taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue-maximizing criterion: set tax rates mindful of elasticity; lowering excessive duties can increase declared trade and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: High duties encourage smuggling and reduce customs revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The high duties which have been imposed upon the importation of many different sorts of foreign goods... have, in many cases, served only to encourage smuggling, and, in all cases, have reduced the revenues of the customs below what more moderate duties would have afforded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: weigh enforcement costs and smuggling incentives when setting tariffs; consider lowering rates or improving administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties and drawbacks encourage fraud and waste public revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The bounties which are sometimes given upon the exportation of home produce and manufactures, and the drawbacks which are paid upon the re-exportation of the greater part of foreign goods, have given occasion to many frauds... The defalcation of the revenue of customs occasioned by bounties and drawbacks... is very great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence (figures provided) shows substantial revenue leakage from bounties/drawbacks. Criterion: design bounties/drawbacks carefully; monitor for fraud and administrative cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile/monopolistic duties distort trade and revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The mercantile system has not been very favourable to the revenue of the great body of the people... In consequence of that system, the importation of several sorts of goods has been prohibited altogether... The high duties... have served only to encourage smuggling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: protectionist prohibitions and monopolistic duties can shrink taxable trade and harm overall welfare and long-term revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical discrimination in customs (alien vs domestic merchants)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gains of alien merchants were looked upon more unfavourably than those of English merchants. It was natural, therefore, that those of the former should be taxed more heavily than those of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes origin of discriminatory duties in ignorance and monopoly spirit; criterion for fair taxation: avoid arbitrary distinctions that encourage inefficiency or rent-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative remedy: reduce smuggling by improving customs administration (excise-like system)
rubrics_metrics.description: The excise laws, it appears, I believe, from experience, obstruct and embarrass the operations of the smuggler much more effectually than those of the customs. By introducing into the customs a system of administration as similar to that of the excise as the nature of the different duties will admit, the difficulty of smuggling might be very much increased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: adapt excise administrative features (clear rules, inspection/warehouse control) to customs where feasible; example: allowing private warehouses under custom-house officer key to control goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate customs duties on a few widely consumed foreign articles
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that the greater part of the members of any society should contribute to the public revenue, in proportion to their respective expense, it does not seem necessary that every single article of that expense should be taxed... It has been the opinion of many people, that, by proper management, the duties of customs might likewise... be confined to a few articles only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy guideline: focus customs on a limited set of commonly consumed foreign goods (examples given: wines, sugar, rum, tobacco, tea, coffee, china-ware, spices) to simplify administration and reduce distortions.
